newsitem.title: SWEDEN: U.S. troubleshooter Holbrooke takes up Baltic role.
newsitem.headline: U.S. troubleshooter Holbrooke takes up Baltic role.

text.p: U.S. troubleshooter Richard Holbrooke takes up a new advisory role on Baltic security on Wednesday when he joins a Baltic Sea council examining the wishes of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to join Western bodies.

Holbrooke, former U.S. assistant Secretary of State, agreed last month to join the Swedish-sponsored advisory board on Baltic Sea cooperation when Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson visited U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington.
The young Baltic states are anxious to reinforce links with the West after quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991.
All three are seeking to join the European Union (EU) or the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) as it enlarges.

The issue of Baltic security is being treated as a priority by Persson and with strong interest by Clinton, who face a dilemma on how to handle the foreign policy wishes of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia. Scandinavian and Western nations are keen to keep them away from the Russian sphere of influence they escaped from five years ago but are hesitating about allowing them full entry to the the EU or NATO.
A spokesman for Persson said Holbrooke was one of 10 members on the council and would advise on a number of areas, particularly investment, drawing on his Wall Street experience.
"Cooperation on investment is good for the security of the region," Persson's spokesman Leif Ake Falk told Reuters.
A spokesman for the U.S. embassy said Holbrooke, widely credited with driving a peace plan for Bosnia, was appointed to the council in a private, not an official, capacity.
Joseph Kruzich from the U.S. Information Service in Stockholm said the U.S. government was organising a diplomatic conference about NATO enlargement in Sweden on November 19.
Over 50 government representatives from the United States, Britain, Russia, Baltics, Poland, Finland, and Sweden, will attend.
"Sometime next year the alliance will make known its decision on which countries it will enter into discussions with on eventual membership," Kruzich told Reuters.
"That will have consequences for Baltic security and countries around the region and we want to prepare the ground for what our policy will be in the region."
